{{Short description|Group-theoretic concept}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] fields of [[category theory]] and [[abstract algebra]], a '''subquotient''' is a [[quotient object]] of a [[subobject]]. Subquotients are particularly important in [[abelian categories]], and in [[group theory]], where they are also known as '''sections''', though this conflicts with [[section (category theory)|a different meaning]] in category theory.

So in the [[algebraic structure]] of groups, <math>H</math> is a subquotient of <math>G</math> if there exists a [[subgroup]] <math>G'</math> of <math>G</math> and a [[normal subgroup]] <math>G''</math> of <math>G'</math> so that <math>H</math> is [[isomorphic]] to <math>G'/G''</math>.

In the literature about [[sporadic groups]] wordings like "<math>H</math> is involved in <math>G</math>"<ref>{{citation |author-link=Robert Griess |last=Griess |first=Robert L. |title=The Friendly Giant|page=1−102|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|volume=69|year=1982|doi=10.1007/BF01389186|bibcode=1982InMat..69....1G |hdl=2027.42/46608 |s2cid=123597150 |url=https://www.digizeitschriften.de/dms/img/?PPN=PPN356556735_0069&DMDID=dmdlog7|hdl-access=free}}</ref> can be found with the apparent meaning of "<math>H</math> is a subquotient of <math>G</math>".

As in the context of subgroups, in the context of subquotients the term ''trivial'' may be used for the two subquotients <math>G</math> and <math> \{1\} </math> which are present in every group <math>G</math>.{{citation needed|date=January 2024}}

A quotient of a subrepresentation of a representation (of, say, a group) might be called a subquotient representation; e.&thinsp;g., [[Harish-Chandra]]'s subquotient theorem.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Dixmier | first1=Jacques |author-link=Jacques Dixmier | title=Enveloping algebras | orig-year=1974 | url=https://books.google.com/books?isbn=0821805606 | publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]] | location=Providence, R.I. | series=[[Graduate Studies in Mathematics]] | isbn=978-0-8218-0560-2 | mr=0498740 | year=1996 | volume=11}} p. 310</ref>

==Example==
There are subquotients of groups which are neither a subgroup nor a quotient of it. For example, according to the article [[Sporadic group#Third generation (8 groups): other subgroups of the Monster|Sporadic group]], ''Fi''<sub>22</sub> has a double cover which is a subgroup of ''Fi''<sub>23</sub>, so it is a subquotient of ''Fi''<sub>23</sub> without being a subgroup or quotient of it.

==Order relation==
The relation ''subquotient of'' is an [[Partially ordered set#Partial orders|order relation]], which shall be denoted by <math>\preceq</math>. It shall be proved for groups.

;Notation
:Let {{Mvar|G}} be a group, let {{Math|''G''&prime;}} be a subgroup of {{Mvar|G}}, let {{Math|''G''&prime;&prime;}} be a normal subgroup of {{Math|''G''&prime;}}, and let {{Mvar|H}} be the quotient group {{Math|''G''&prime; / ''G''&prime;&prime;}}.  Then we say that {{Mvar|H}} is a subquotient of {{Mvar|G}}.  In symbols, let {{Math|''G''&prime;&prime; &#9667; ''G''&prime; &le; ''G''}} and {{Math|1=''H'' = ''G''&prime; / ''G''&prime;&prime;}}; then {{Math|''H'' &#10927; ''G''}}.  This relationship has the following properties:

# [[Reflexive relation|Reflexivity]]: <math>G\preceq G</math>, i.&thinsp;e. every element is related to itself. Indeed, <math>G</math> is isomorphic to the subquotient <math>G/\{1\}</math> of <math>G</math>.
# [[Antisymmetric relation|Antisymmetry]]: if <math>G\preceq H</math> and <math>H\preceq G</math> then <math>G\cong H</math>; that is, no two distinct elements precede each other. Indeed, a comparison of the group orders of <math>G</math> and <math>H</math> then yields <math>|G| = |H|</math> from which <math>G\cong H</math>.
# [[Transitive relation|Transitivity]]: if <math>H'/H'' \preceq H</math> and <math>H\preceq G</math> then <math>H'/H'' \preceq G</math>.

===Proof of transitivity for groups===
Let <math>H'/H''</math> be a subquotient of <math>H</math>, let <math>H := G'/G''</math> be a subquotient of <math>G</math>, and let <math>\varphi \colon G' \to H</math> be the [[canonical homomorphism]]. Then in the following diagram, all vertical (<math>\downarrow</math>) maps <math>\varphi \colon X \to Y, \; x \mapsto x \, G''</math>
{|style="text-align:center;"
|-
|style="width:6em;"| &nbsp; ||
|style="width:2.3em;"| <math>G''</math> ||style="width:6.1em;"| <math>\leq</math> ||style="width:5.4em;"| <math>\varphi^{-1}(H'')</math> ||style="width:2.5em;"| <math>\leq</math> ||style="width:6.4em;"| <math>\varphi^{-1}(H')</math> ||style="width:2.63em;"| <math>\vartriangleleft</math> ||style="width:7em;"| <math>G'</math>||
|-
| ||style="width:2.4em;"| <math>\varphi\!:</math> || <math>\Big\downarrow</math> || || <math>\Big\downarrow</math> || || <math>\Big\downarrow</math> || || <math>\Big\downarrow</math>
|-
| || || <math>\{1\}</math> || <math>\leq</math> || <math>H''</math> || <math>\vartriangleleft</math> || <math>H'</math> || <math>\vartriangleleft</math> || <math>H</math>
|}
are [[surjective function|surjective]] for the respective pairs
{|style="text-align:center;"
|-
|style="width:1.4em;"| ||style="text-align:right;"| <math>(X,Y) \; \; \; \in</math> ||style="width:6.7em;"| <math>\Bigl\{\bigl(G'', \{1\}\bigr) \Bigr.</math> ||<math>,</math> ||style="width:8.8em;"| <math>\bigl(\varphi^{-1}(H''),H''\bigr)</math> || <math>,</math> || style="width:9.2em;"| <math>\bigl(\varphi^{-1}(H'),H'\bigr)</math> ||<math>,</math> || style="width:8em;"| <math>\Bigl.\bigl(G',H\bigr)\Bigr\} .</math>
|}
The [[preimage]]s <math>\varphi^{-1}\left(H'\right)</math> and <math>\varphi^{-1}\left(H''\right)</math> are both subgroups of <math>G'</math> containing <math>G'' ,</math> and it is <math>\varphi\left(\varphi^{-1}\left(H'\right)\right) = H'</math> and <math>\varphi\left(\varphi^{-1}\left(H''\right)\right) = H'',</math> because every <math>h \in H</math> has a preimage <math>g \in G'</math> with <math>\varphi(g) = h .</math> Moreover, the  subgroup <math>\varphi^{-1}\left(H''\right) </math> is normal in <math>\varphi^{-1}\left(H'\right) .</math>

As a consequence, the subquotient <math>H'/H''</math> of <math>H</math> is a subquotient of <math>G</math> of the form <math>H'/H'' \cong \varphi^{-1}\left(H'\right)/\varphi^{-1}\left(H''\right) .</math>

===Relation to cardinal order===
In [[constructive set theory]], where the [[law of excluded middle]] does not necessarily hold, one can consider the relation ''subquotient of'' as replacing the usual [[order relation]](s) on [[cardinal number|cardinals]]. When one has the law of the excluded middle, then a subquotient <math>Y</math> of <math>X</math> is either the [[empty set]] or there is an onto function <math>X\to Y</math>. This order relation is traditionally denoted <math>\leq^\ast .</math> If additionally the [[axiom of choice]] holds, then <math>Y</math> has a one-to-one function to <math>X</math> and this order relation is the usual <math>\leq</math> on corresponding cardinals.
